title_original: Victor Ehikhamenor: What Remains When a City Disappears?
excerpt_original: At the Penelope Gallery, Chau Chak Wing Museum, University of Sydney, Nigerian-American artist and writer Victor Ehikhamenor transforms discarded objects and fragments of domestic life into a meditation on displacement, cultural memory and the enduring […]

blocks.text: At the Penelope Gallery, Chau Chak Wing Museum, University of Sydney, Nigerian-American artist and writer Victor Ehikhamenor transforms discarded objects and fragments of domestic life into a meditation on displacement, cultural memory and the enduring meaning of home.

Cities can erase entire neighbourhoods, but they cannot so easily extinguish the lives, memories and histories embedded within them. A discarded mirror, a worn piece of clothing, an abandoned drawer — objects once integral to someone’s daily existence become powerful reminders of what is lost, carried away or reconstructed elsewhere. For Nigerian-American artist and writer Victor Ehikhamenor, these remnants of domestic life hold the emotional weight of displacement and the persistence of belonging. In his first Australian solo exhibition, Undoing the City: Making Home , he brings the changing urban landscapes of Sydney, Cairo and Port Harcourt into dialogue, revealing how redevelopment, migration and environmental degradation reshape not only the places people inhabit but also their understanding of who they are. Victor Ehikhamenor, Numinous Night (2026). Image courtesy of Chau Chak Wing Museum.

blocks.caption: Victor Ehikhamenor, Numinous Night (2026). Image courtesy of Chau Chak Wing Museum.

blocks.text: Drawing on two years of collaborative research, Ehikhamenor creates installations in which personal memory intersects with larger histories of migration, colonial trade and environmental change. Works including Uwa Uwa , He Left, and Not Home consider the distinction between a house and a home, exploring the cultural practices, relationships and memories that accompany people across geographical boundaries. His upbringing in Nigeria’s Edo State informs an artistic language in which everyday materials coexist with spiritual references and inherited traditions. At the heart of his practice is a simple observation: “ you do not travel with your house, but you travel with your home.” In this interview with Suzette Bell-Roberts, Ehikhamenor reflects on the histories embedded in ordinary objects, the complexities of belonging and his encounters with emerging African-diaspora creatives in Western Sydney.
Suzette Bell-Roberts: ‘Undoing the City: Making Home’ explores urban transformation, displacement and belonging. What drew you to these themes, and how did they shape your approach to the exhibition?

Victor Ehikhamenor: What interested me was the question of what happens to our understanding of home when the places we inhabit begin to change. A city is never static. It is constantly evolving, sometimes through natural processes, sometimes through development, and sometimes through environmental degradation and extraction. But when these changes occur, we have to ask what happens to the people who have built their lives around those places.

The exhibition emerged from research conducted over time by two professors working across different locations, including Okrika in the Niger Delta. My role was to engage with that research and consider how to translate its questions into an artistic experience. I was particularly interested in the relationship between physical displacement and the things people carry with them, whether consciously or unconsciously, when they leave a place.

That led me to think about home beyond its physical structures. I began working with domestic objects, used clothing and other materials that could evoke the experience of living somewhere, leaving somewhere and trying to establish oneself elsewhere. Rather than illustrating the research literally, I wanted to create an installation where these questions could be experienced through objects, spaces, and the memories they might awaken.

The exhibition brings together experiences from Sydney, Cairo and Port Harcourt, cities with distinct histories and cultural identities. What connections and differences emerged, and how did they inform the work’s development?

I think the interesting thing about bringing these places together is that you begin to see how different histories can lead us to similar questions. The research draws connections across places with very different cultural, environmental and political circumstances. I did not personally conduct fieldwork in all these locations. Still, my familiarity with Nigeria, particularly the Niger Delta and the broader questions surrounding displacement and extraction, informed how I responded to the research.

In Okrika, for instance, the history of secondhand clothing and the circulation of used goods opens up a conversation about trade, colonial encounters and the movement of materials across borders. In Sydney, I gathered used objects to construct an installation about home and displacement. There is an interesting connection there: objects that have already lived somewhere, that have been used by somebody else, acquire another life when they enter a new environment.

Of course, the histories of these places are not interchangeable. Each has its own particular circumstances, and it is important not to flatten those differences. But when you look at how people relate to their homes, what they remember and what they carry when they move, you begin to recognise certain shared human experiences.

For me, the exhibition is about letting these histories speak to one another without insisting they are the same. The connections become meaningful precisely because the differences remain. Victor Ehikhamenor, So Far (2026). Image courtesy of the Chau Chak Wing Museum.

blocks.caption: Victor Ehikhamenor, So Far (2026). Image courtesy of the Chau Chak Wing Museum.

blocks.text: The idea of home extends beyond physical structures to memory, identity and cultural belonging. How do you understand home, and how has that understanding evolved through your artistic practice?

There is a saying from my place that you do not travel with your house, but you travel with your home. I think that captures it quite well. A house is a physical structure, but home is something much more complicated. It has to do with the people around you, the things you remember, the food you eat, the language you speak and the experiences that shape your understanding of yourself.

Growing up in Edo State, certain memories and realities stay with you, no matter where you eventually end up. You might leave the village or move to another country, but you continue to carry aspects of that upbringing. When people migrate, they often seek out others from their communities, recreate familiar rituals, prepare familiar food and establish spaces where they can experience something of what they have left behind.

This understanding informed the installation Uwa Uwa , which means “home is home.” Through domestic objects and familiar materials, I considered how people recreate a sense of home in places that are physically different from where they come from. Other parts of the installation, including He Left and Not Home , explore the ambiguities of leaving, absence and the attempt to belong somewhere.

I think my artistic practice has made me increasingly conscious that home is not always something we can define neatly. Sometimes it is a place, sometimes it is a memory, and sometimes it is a feeling we are still trying to recover or recreate.

Your work frequently draws on the visual and spiritual traditions of the historic Benin Kingdom. How have these traditions influenced your exploration of cultural memory and the changing urban landscape in this exhibition?

My upbringing in Edo State has always informed how I see and interpret the world. You cannot simply separate yourself from the visual traditions, cultural practices and histories that shaped you. They become part of your sensibility, even when you are working with subjects that extend beyond your immediate cultural environment.

In this exhibition, those influences appear alongside materials and references that speak to domestic life, migration and displacement. The amulets beneath the stained glass, for instance, carry cultural and spiritual associations that may be immediately recognisable to some viewers but less familiar to others. I want these different references to coexist within the installation rather than explain everything away.

At the same time, I would not say that the exhibition is simply about the traditions of the Benin Kingdom. It is responding to a broader body of research, and my own cultural background is one of the perspectives I bring to that engagement. The question is how we carry our histories into new environments and how those histories continue to shape our understanding of belonging.

For me, cultural memory is not something that exists only in the past. It continues to operate in the present, in the objects we keep, the rituals we practise and the ways we make meaning of unfamiliar spaces. That continuity shapes how I approach the work. Victor Ehikhamenor, Undoing the City (2026). Image courtesy of the Chau Chak Wing Museum.

blocks.caption: Victor Ehikhamenor, Undoing the City (2026). Image courtesy of the Chau Chak Wing Museum.

blocks.text: Throughout your practice, you have worked with rosary beads, perforated paper, bronze and symbolic imagery. How do you approach the relationship between material, memory and storytelling, and what role do these elements play in ‘Undoing the City: Making Home’?

I think the first thing to understand is that materials already have lives before they enter an artwork. They have histories, associations and uses that precede whatever the artist decides to do with them. I am interested in what happens when you take something out of its familiar context and place it somewhere else, allowing it to acquire another meaning without necessarily losing what it carried before.

A large part of Undoing the City: Making Home is made from used objects. When I went looking for materials in Sydney, I was interested in things that had already been lived with, things that had a history. A drawer, a tie, a mirror or an ordinary household item might seem unremarkable, but these objects can contain traces of everyday life. They can remind us of particular people, homes and experiences.

The material also relates to the histories it connects us to. The idea of Okrika, for instance, brings the circulation of secondhand goods into the conversation. Objects move between places, take on different uses, and take on new lives. In that sense, the materials themselves participate in the storytelling.

I do not necessarily approach an object with a single meaning already fixed in my mind. Sometimes its significance emerges through the process of working with it and considering its relationship to other elements in the installation. I am interested in creating a situation where the material can speak through its physical presence, its history and the associations it evokes in the viewer.

The exhibition emerges from collaborative research into communities experiencing significant urban change. How did you approach these communities’ stories and experiences, and what guided you in translating them into artistic form?

My starting point was to engage with the research already conducted and consider how I could respond to it through my own artistic sensibility. The research covered different locations and experiences, and I did not approach the exhibition as though I could speak directly for every community represented. Instead, I focused on questions I could explore through material, memory, and the experience of domestic space.

One thing I kept returning to was the recognition that displacement is experienced differently by different people, but the emotions surrounding it can resonate across those differences. You may not have lived in somebody else’s community or experienced exactly what they have. Still, you can recognise the longing for home, the anxiety of leaving or the desire to preserve something of the life you knew.

That understanding informed my choice of materials. I used objects that had already been part of people’s lives, bringing them together with drawings and other elements to construct an environment that could suggest the intimacy of a home while also raising questions about absence and dislocation.

I also made practical and conceptual decisions about what belonged in the exhibition. Not everything I gathered or considered making eventually found its place in the installation. I had to think about how the different elements worked together and whether they contributed to the questions I was trying to explore.

More significantly, I wanted the work to remain open to different interpretations. The installation draws on specific research and histories, but it also creates room for viewers to bring their own experiences into the encounter. Victor Ehikhamenor, Undoing the City (2026). Image courtesy of the Chau Chak Wing Museum.

blocks.caption: Victor Ehikhamenor, Undoing the City (2026). Image courtesy of the Chau Chak Wing Museum.

blocks.text: Alongside the exhibition, you are mentoring emerging African and African-descended creatives in Western Sydney through a programme developed with Blacktown Arts. What has this exchange brought to your understanding of artistic practice, community and the transmission of knowledge across generations?

One of the most valuable aspects of the programme has been the opportunity to encounter people whose experiences and perspectives differ from mine. Participants work across different disciplines, including photography, filmmaking, radio, fine art, and digital art. They also have different relationships with migration and belonging. Some arrived in Australia when they were young, while others were born there and have never necessarily had the opportunity to return to their families’ countries of origin.

Listening to them has reminded me that there is no single way to experience cultural identity. Even when people share a geographical or cultural background, their relationships with that heritage can differ greatly.

One participant, a young radio presenter from Sudan, researched Nigerian rock music in the period following the Civil War. She explored how the political and historical circumstances of that time contributed to the emergence of a particular musical culture. I found her research eye-opening because she approached a history I knew from a different perspective and highlighted connections I hadn’t considered in quite the same way.

I have always believed that mentorship is a reciprocal process. You may enter a room as the person expected to share knowledge, but that doesn’t mean you are the only person with something to offer. You must be willing to learn from the people you are mentoring.

The programme has also allowed the participants to follow my process, from the early stages of gathering materials to the development of the installation. I think that exchange is important because artistic knowledge is not transmitted only through formal instruction. Sometimes it comes through observation, conversation, questioning and the willingness to remain open to another person’s way of thinking.

Your practice has long engaged with cultural heritage, colonial histories and contemporary identity. How does Undoing the City: Making Home contribute to this ongoing exploration, and what new questions has the project opened for you?

I think the exhibition brings several strands of my practice into conversation. I have always been interested in the histories that objects carry, the ways people relate to their past, and how those histories continue to shape contemporary life. In this project, those concerns come together through the question of home and what happens when the spaces associated with it begin to change.

The history of used clothing in Nigeria, for instance, connects an ordinary object to much larger questions of trade, colonial encounters and the movement of goods between different parts of the world. When I gather used objects in Sydney, I work with materials that already have histories, even if I do not know all the details. Bringing them into the installation allows me to consider how objects move between contexts and how their meanings change along the way.

The project has also reinforced the relationship between my writing and my visual art. In my forthcoming collection of short stories, Central Hotel , I explore questions of migration, dislocation and the experience of living between worlds. One of the stories, “Waiting for the Budoza,” speaks to concerns that are also present in this exhibition. I have reached a point where my writing and visual practice increasingly converge around certain ideas, even when the forms of expression are different.

The exhibition continues to open up for me the question of what we carry when we leave a place, and what happens to those things when we try to establish ourselves somewhere else. How much of home can be reconstructed? What remains when the physical environment changes? And how do the memories we carry influence the new places we create for ourselves?
I do not think these questions have straightforward answers. But I think art lets us return to them, approach them from different directions, and discover new meanings through the process.
This exhibition is on view from 15 October 2026 to 26 April 2027 at the Penelope Gallery , Level 1, Chau Chak Wing Museum, University of Sydney, Australia.
